st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The decision strongly accepts the cluster’s human-led, verification-centred approach and materially develops it into concrete legal duties. It holds that existing procedural and ethical rules apply regardless of how work is produced, requires filing lawyers personally to read and verify authorities, and preserves professional judgment and accountability rather than treating nominal human involvement as sufficient.
qs: However legal papers are prepared, and however legal technology develops, our procedural and ethical rules apply with equal force.

“Simply stated, no brief, pleading, motion, or any other paper filed in any court should contain any citations—whether provided by generative AI or any other source—that the attorney responsible for submitting the pleading has not personally read and verified.” Noland, 114 Cal.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: generative AI may appropriately assist legal practice, but responsibility remains with the lawyer and unchecked output creates heightened ethical and procedural risk. Its emphasis on rigorous verification and present risks from fabrications and inaccuracies aligns with the synthesis, though it does not materially address the broader division among courts over disclosure, certification and prohibition.
qs: While not inherently unethical or irresponsible, using generative AI without rigorously checking its output does present a higher risk of violating certain ethical and procedural rules.
Two types of mistakes, or “hallucinations,” are most relevant: fabrications and inaccuracies.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Lnu v. Blanche directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between fabricated citations and misleading uses of genuine authorities. It also reinforces that lawyers must closely verify AI-assisted legal work themselves, while treating reported error rates as task- and time-specific rather than fixed.
qs: The generative AI tool might cite to real authorities but provide an answer that is legally or factually inaccurate or not supported by the citation.

kp.k: Discipline targets inaccurate filings, not AI use itself
kp.d: The court expressly declines to sanction the mere use of generative AI. Its disciplinary analysis generally turns on signing and filing fabricated or unsupported material, irrespective of whether humans or technology produced it; the source of errors matters separately to candor. The order applies existing appellate and California professional rules rather than establishing a general prohibition on AI-assisted drafting.
qs: We do not sanction Sethi and Rounds for the simple fact that they or their subordinates used generative AI.
That is, the rules are not violated at the point of research and drafting, but at the point of signing and filing.
However legal papers are prepared, and however legal technology develops, our procedural and ethical rules apply with equal force.

kp.k: Verification requires substantive legal judgment, not citation existence checks
kp.d: The court requires the submitting attorney to read cited authorities and check their existence, attribution, and substantive support. Drawing on California guidance and Noland, it explains that competence and diligence require reasoning about authorities, beyond screening out fabricated citations or checking topical relevance. This professional judgment cannot be delegated to AI and applies equally to filings prepared without AI.
qs: the party or attorney who submits the filing with this Court must read the authorities cited therein to ensure that they are real, properly attributed, and accurately represented.
A competent and diligent attorney must also read and reason.
This exercise of professional judgment “cannot be delegated to generative AI and remains the lawyer’s responsibility at all times.”

kp.k: Delegated drafting does not transfer signing attorneys' responsibility
kp.d: The firm assigned legal arguments and supporting authority to unlicensed law-school graduates while attorneys prepared facts and normally did not vet citations. The court finds that reliance on subordinates and claimed ignorance of their AI use do not excuse Sethi, the sole brief signatory. It additionally suggests, without deciding, that the delegation system may have violated California nonlawyer-supervision and unauthorized-practice rules. The attorneys reported hiring a licensed attorney to read future briefs.
qs: While the statement of facts for each brief is prepared by an attorney, the Brief Writers are left to write the legal arguments and identify supporting authority for those arguments.
It is no excuse that Sethi entrusted substantive cite checking to subordinates, and it is no excuse that Sethi purportedly did not know his subordinates had used generative AI.
the Firm’s system of delegation may have violated California’s responsibilities for supervising nonlawyers and its prohibition on the unauthorized practice of law.

kp.k: False authorities produced concrete procedural and ethical violations
kp.d: The opening brief contained two nonexistent cases and quotations absent from the cited opinions; the reply and other pending matters contained further fabricated or misrepresented authorities. The court finds Sethi violated appellate citation requirements and California duties of competence, diligence, and presenting meritorious claims. Possible support from uncited cases, or the contention that affected points were minor, did not excuse the filings. The underlying petition for review had nevertheless been granted on November 4, 2025.
qs: Sethi filed an opening brief in this case with multiple fabricated citations and quotations.
It is irrelevant that other cases may stand for the propositions asserted.
And all claims in a brief, no matter how minor, must be made with citations to real authority or a good faith argument for a change in the law.

kp.k: Misinterpretations of real authorities create less visible AI risks
kp.d: The court distinguishes nonexistent authorities and quotations from inaccurate answers citing real authorities. Adopting the cited Magesh study's broader use of 'hallucinations,' it argues that substantive inaccuracies may be more dangerous in the long run because superficial checks miss them. This is the court's risk assessment, not a measured comparative harm finding; identified error modes include misunderstood holdings, rejected party arguments presented as holdings, and disregard of authority hierarchies.
qs: The generative AI tool might cite to real authorities but provide an answer that is legally or factually inaccurate or not supported by the citation.
Fabrications are the most notorious hallucinations, but inaccuracies may prove more dangerous to our profession in the long run.
Inaccuracies are more likely to go unnoticed by attorneys and judges because they are not always susceptible to facial checks.

kp.k: Reported tool error rates concern 2024 queries
kp.d: Citing Magesh et al., Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools (2025), the court reports hallucinations, including substantive inaccuracies, in 17% of Westlaw answers and 33% of Lexis answers to a representative query set run in 2024. These are reported research findings, not error rates measured in this litigation. The court expressly allows that subsequent improvements may have reduced rates, while quoting the study's caution that advanced legal-specific models are unlikely to eliminate the problem entirely.
qs: Including inaccuracies, legal-specific generative AI tools from Westlaw and Lexis hallucinated 17% and 33% of answers, respectively, to a representative set of queries run in 2024.
Generative AI is improving rapidly, so it is possible that these hallucination rates have decreased.

kp.k: Candor requires prompt disclosure of errors and their origins
kp.d: The court requires immediate notification to the court and opposing counsel, identification of the kind of error, and disclosure of its source. It finds that replacing a fabricated case with a real citation without revealing the fabrication fails to correct the previous representation that the case existed. It also emphasizes acknowledging uncertainty instead of categorically denying AI use without a factual basis.
qs: An attorney who erroneously submits a hallucination in a brief must notify the Court and opposing counsel immediately, describe the nature of the error (a fabrication, a gross misrepresentation, etc.), and disclose how the error came about—here, misused generative AI.
Swapping a hallucination out for a real case does not correct the prior false claim that “this is a real case.”
Candor requires admissions of uncertainty just as much as it requires revealing facts known for certain.

kp.k: Firm AI bans do not excuse unsupported denials
kp.d: The attorneys initially characterized fabricated citations as typographical or copy-paste errors and invoked the firm's AI prohibition to explain their belief. They subsequently conceded unauthorized AI use and failed cite-checking were 'more likely than not' or 'probable.' The court inferred knowing misrepresentations from the circumstances and rejected the policy as an excuse; its findings did not depend on a documented reconstruction of which tool generated the errors.
qs: Notwithstanding these explanations and arguments, Sethi and Rounds now concede it is “more likely than not” or “probable” that the errors were the product of unauthorized AI use by their Brief Writers and a failure to cite check.
The fact of any such policy, which Sethi and Rounds did not attach in written form to their Response, is irrelevant.
We thus infer from the circumstances that Sethi and Rounds knew as early as the Motion to Correct that the errors were not innocent typographical or copy-paste errors.

kp.k: Repeated concealment materially increased professional discipline
kp.d: The court attributes the severity of discipline to repeated candor failures and states that transparent disclosure and an apology at the correction stage might have justified lesser sanctions. It imposes a personal $2,500 sanction on each lawyer and a six-month suspension from Ninth Circuit practice beginning ten days after filing. It also requires dissemination to clients, opposing counsel, presiding judges in pending cases, and firm attorneys, with referral to licensing authorities.
qs: The gravity of discipline we impose, including the temporary suspension of practice, is owed to this repeated failure of candor.
Sethi and Rounds are each personally sanctioned in the amount of $2,500.
Sethi and Rounds are hereby suspended from practice before this Court for a period of six months starting ten days after this Order is filed.

kp.k: Firm-wide AI disclosure and verification certification imposed
kp.d: As a case-specific disciplinary measure, the order requires Sethi, Rounds, and every firm attorney to include sworn statements in all future filings for two years identifying whether generative AI was used, naming the tool, and certifying personal review and the existence of cited and quoted authority. This is a firm-wide remedial obligation, not an announced disclosure requirement for all Ninth Circuit practitioners.
qs: Sethi, Rounds, and all attorneys at the Firm are ordered to include in all future filings a statement, made under penalty of perjury, addressing whether generative AI was used, disclosing the name of the tool used, and certifying that the attorney signing the brief or other filing has personally reviewed the filing and that all citations and quotations therein refer to existing authority.
This requirement shall remain in place for two years from the date of this Order.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The panel identifies increased accuracy risks from unchecked generative AI, but holds that AI does not displace lawyers’ existing verification, professional judgment, or candor obligations.
pts.d: The Ninth Circuit panel (Paez, Bea and Forrest) states that using generative AI without rigorous checking increases the risk of ethical and procedural violations. It distinguishes fabricated authorities from subtler inaccuracies involving real authorities, predicting that the latter may be more dangerous over time because attorneys and judges are less likely to detect them. The panel does not prohibit AI-assisted research or drafting: responsibility attaches to signing and filing inaccurate work, regardless of whether the source is AI or a human. Lawyers must personally read cited authorities and assess their substantive relevance; merely confirming that cases exist is insufficient. When errors emerge, lawyers must promptly disclose their nature and source, acknowledging uncertainty rather than categorically denying possible AI use. The order makes no productivity, employment, or market-size prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The panel relies on documented filing errors and admissions, a cited empirical study of legal research tools, and procedural and professional-conduct authorities.
pts.d: The order documents nonexistent cases, misattributed quotations, and substantive misrepresentations in Lnu and identifies similar problems in two other pending immigration cases. The attorneys admitted that they did not normally vet their brief writers’ citations and later characterized unauthorized AI use as probable; the panel inferred knowledge and misconduct from the circumstances rather than presenting model logs or a controlled investigation identifying the drafting tool. For broader reliability claims, the panel cites Magesh et al., Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools (2025), reporting 17% and 33% hallucination rates for Westlaw and Lexis tools respectively on queries run in 2024, including substantive inaccuracies. These are cited study results, not error rates measured from this litigation. The panel expressly adopts that study’s broader definition of hallucination. Its conclusions about responsibility rely on the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, Ninth Circuit rules and advisory guidance, California professional-conduct rules and bar guidance, and prior sanctions decisions including Noland and Mata. Possible violations of nonlawyer-supervision and unauthorized-practice rules are qualified as possibilities, not independently established findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 3, 2026 order qualifies its reliability assessment by technological stage and 2024 data, while treating lawyers’ responsibility as continuing regardless of technological change.
pts.d: The panel ties heightened risks to generative AI’s current stage of advancement and acknowledges that rapid improvement may have reduced the reported 2024 error rates. Its suggestion that inaccuracies may become more dangerous is a qualified long-run prediction, not an observed trend with a specified endpoint. Its legal conclusions concern submitting inaccurate work, not using AI itself, and it expressly distinguishes the identified errors from ordinary minor typographical mistakes. Disclosure is required immediately upon discovering an error. The panel states that prompt disclosure and apology might have justified lesser sanctions; the severity imposed here reflects repeated failures of candor. The six-month suspensions begin ten days after filing of the order, and the firm-wide AI disclosure and personal-review certification requirement lasts two years from the order’s date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects fall on two immigration attorneys and their firm; the wider warning concerns signing lawyers, subordinate brief writers, courts, opposing counsel, and clients.
pts.d: The case concerns an Orange County immigration firm employing unlicensed law-school graduates to draft legal arguments and identify supporting authorities. The panel holds that delegation and an asserted internal AI ban do not excuse a signing attorney’s failure to read and verify those authorities. Sethi and Rounds each receive a $2,500 personal sanction and a six-month suspension from Ninth Circuit practice. All attorneys at their firm must make specified AI-use disclosures and personal-review certifications in future filings for two years. The attorneys must distribute the order to clients, opposing counsel, presiding judges in their pending cases, and firm attorneys; licensing authorities also receive it for possible further proceedings. The panel warns the broader Ninth Circuit bar against overreliance on AI. Courts and opposing counsel are entitled to prompt correction rather than being left to detect unsupported authorities. The underlying petition for review was granted, so the order does not establish that the AI-related errors caused the clients to lose their immigration appeal.
